# 1 Samuel 13 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

## v. 1 — Saul’s Age and Reign

**Traditional reading:** This verse follows the standard formula for introducing a king’s reign (cf. 2 Sam 5:4; 1 Kgs 14:21; 2 Kgs 8:26). Saul was either 30 or 40 years old when he began to reign and reigned 40 or 42 years total.

**The Hebrew text is defective here.** The Masoretic Text literally reads “Saul was a son of a year when he began to reign, and he reigned two years over Israel,” which is impossible. The Septuagint omits the verse altogether. Some Greek manuscripts supply “thirty years,” the Syriac has “twenty-one,” and the ASV/NASB supply “forty.” Paul in Acts 13:21 says Saul reigned forty years. Most modern translations (NIV, NLT, CSB, BSB) reconstruct “thirty years old…forty-two years” based on a combination of manuscript evidence and Paul’s round number of forty. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-13-commentary; https://www.studylight.org/interlinear-study-bible/hebrew/1-samuel/13-1.html)

**Ellicott:** The corruption or gap in the text dates from a far-back period. The English translation is a probable but conjectural paraphrase. The usually accepted meaning is that Saul had reigned one year when the events of ch. 12 took place, and after he had reigned two years total he chose the 3,000 men described in v. 2. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/13.htm)

**Gill:** Some rabbis interpreted it figuratively—“Saul was as innocent as a one-year-old child when he began to reign.” Others reckoned from his unction at Ramah or his election at Mizpeh. The Jewish chronologers made the whole reign only two years, which is improbable given all the events recorded. Josephus says he reigned 18 years in Samuel’s lifetime and 22 after his death—40 total, matching Acts 13:21. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/13.htm)

**Precept Austin / NET Notes:** The MT does not have “thirty.” A number has dropped out—as it stands, the MT literally says Saul was one year old. Some scholars prefer “forty” because Jonathan was already a military commander in v. 2. The BSB’s “thirty…forty-two” is a possible but uncertain proposal. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-13-commentary)

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** The original inspired manuscript probably gave Saul’s age and length of reign as with other kings. The NASB supplies “forty” and “thirty-two,” but neither number is in the extant manuscripts. It is impossible to understand the exact import today. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-samuel-13.html)

---

## v. 2 — Saul Assembles Israel’s First Standing Army

**Traditional reading:** Saul chose 3,000 men as a permanent regular force—Israel’s first standing army. Previously, Israel had only a militia that mustered in times of national threat. Two thousand were stationed with Saul at Michmash (a strategic position about 9 miles NE of Jerusalem) and in the hill country of Bethel; one thousand were with Jonathan at Gibeah of Benjamin (Saul’s hometown). The rest he sent home.

**Guzik (Enduring Word):** This was Israel’s first “regular” army. Previously Israel only had a militia. This is also the first mention of Jonathan, whom Clarke called “one of the most amiable characters in the Bible.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-13/)

**Ellicott:** Saul’s military genius and foresight are seen here—this standing army was the first step toward developing Israel into a great military power. It enabled David and Solomon’s later conquests. Saul wisely saw that Israel was not yet trained or armed for a full-scale war with the Philistines. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/13.htm)

**Gill:** These 3,000 men were chosen from the 300,000 who had gone with Saul against the Ammonites. Some were a bodyguard, others a standing army to preserve peace and watch Philistine movements. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/13.htm)

**Precept Austin:** Michmash, Gibeah, and Geba were in close geographic proximity. Understanding this helps explain why Jonathan attacked the Philistine garrison at Geba in v. 3. Saul sent the rest home—surprising given the Philistine garrison was near his hometown. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-13-commentary)

---

## vv. 3–4 — Jonathan Attacks the Philistine Outpost

**Traditional reading:** Jonathan attacked and defeated the Philistine garrison at Geba. Saul then blew the trumpet (shofar) throughout the land to summon Israel to war, saying “Let the Hebrews hear!” The news spread that “Saul” (not Jonathan) had struck the garrison, and Israel had become a stench (“abomination”) to the Philistines. The people were summoned to Saul at Gilgal.

**Guzik:** Jonathan was a remarkable military leader. This attack merely “wakened” the Philistines. Israel had enjoyed the “peace” of a subjected people. Spiritually, the same principle applies: as long as we are weak and subjected to our spiritual enemies, they don’t mind us; but when we show boldness against the LORD’s enemies, we become an abomination to them. Saul plainly took credit for Jonathan’s bold attack—a bad flaw in his character driven by insecurity. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-13/)

**Ellicott:** Jonathan appears as the perfect type of a warrior—first in courage, activity, and speed. His personal beauty and swiftness earned him the name “gazelle” among the troops (cf. 2 Sam 1:19). “Saul” is put for “Jonathan” since Saul was commander-in-chief. Some translate “garrison” as “pillar” (a Philistine authority symbol) or as a proper name for the tribute-collecting officer. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/13.htm)

**Gill:** Jonathan, not Saul, did the smiting, but it was ascribed to Saul as commander. Geba is not the same as Gibeah of Benjamin—both were in Benjamin but were distinct places. The Targum understands this as Jonathan killing a single Philistine governor/tax collector. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/13.htm)

**Precept Austin / Brian Bell:** This represents Saul’s “first step down” on the slippery slope—he failed to act decisively himself (Jonathan did it) and then took the credit. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-13-commentary)

**Archaeological note (Guzik):** The Philistine fortress at Geba (also known as Gibeah) has been found by archaeologists. Evidence shows it was destroyed but later rebuilt by Saul as his palace and fortress. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-13/)

---

## v. 5 — The Philistine Response

**Traditional reading:** The Philistines assembled a massive army: 30,000 chariots, 6,000 horsemen, and infantry “as numerous as the sand on the seashore.” They camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven.

**The number of chariots is widely questioned.** Poole (cited by Guzik) notes the Syriac and Arabic versions read “three thousand,” not “thirty thousand.” Ellicott observes that in all ancient army records, war chariots are always fewer than horsemen—here they are five times as numerous. Pharaoh had only 600 (Exod 14:7), Jabin 900 (Judg 4:3), Solomon 1,400 (1 Kgs 10:26), and Zerah the Ethiopian only 300 (2 Chr 14:9). The more probable reading is 3,000 or even 300. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-13/; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/13.htm)

**Gill:** It may seem incredible for so small a people as the Philistines. Some suggest the word “chariots” means men fighting in chariots (about 10 men per chariot); 3,000 men would fill 300 chariots, proportionate to 6,000 horsemen. Josephus says there were 300,000 footmen. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/13.htm)

---

## vv. 6–7 — Israel’s Fear and Desertion

**Traditional reading:** Seeing the danger, the men of Israel hid in caves, thickets, rocks, cellars (holes), and cisterns (pits). Some Hebrews crossed the Jordan into Gad and Gilead. Saul remained at Gilgal with his troops “quaking in fear.”

**Guzik:** This was a low point for Israel. Many probably thought, “What we really need is a king—a king would solve our problems.” Now they had a king and the problems were still there. God intended to teach them the vanity of carnal confidence in men. Saul stayed at Gilgal—possibly wanting to re-live the glorious day when Samuel confirmed him as king (1 Sam 11:15). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-13/)

**Ellicott:** The panic was caused by the extraordinary size of the Philistine host. Josephus notes foreign allies had joined them. The word translated “high places” in the KJV actually means “towers” or fortified holds—ruins of old Canaanite structures. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/13.htm)

**Gill:** Some Hebrews fled as far as possible—to Gad and Gilead east of the Jordan. Kimchi notes the land of Reuben is not mentioned because it was nearer the Jordan and they wanted to go further for safety. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/13.htm)

**Precept Austin / Brian Bell:** This is Saul’s “second step down”—he failed to inspire the people. Instead of rallying them in faith, he let fear dominate the camp. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-13-commentary)

---

## vv. 8–9 — Saul’s Unlawful Sacrifice

**Traditional reading:** Saul waited seven days “for the time appointed by Samuel” (referring back to 1 Sam 10:8, where Samuel told Saul to wait seven days at Gilgal). But Samuel did not come, and the troops began to desert. So Saul took matters into his own hands: he called for the burnt offering and peace offerings and offered the burnt offering himself.

**Guzik:** Saul’s disobedience stemmed from panic, not confusion. The waiting was stressful because time felt like his enemy, and the people were scattering. He offered the sacrifice himself—plainly sinful on two counts: (1) he disobeyed Samuel’s command, and (2) only priests were to offer sacrifices. King Uzziah later tried the same and was struck with leprosy (2 Chr 26). Trapp: “If Saul was among the prophets before, will he now be among the priests? Can there be any devotion in disobedience?” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-13/)

**Ellicott (important nuance):** Ellicott argues that Saul’s sin was *not* the act of offering sacrifice with his own hand—no unlawful assumption of priestly functions is anywhere charged on Saul (unlike Uzziah in 2 Chr 26:18). It is more than probable that the priest Ahiah, who was in attendance on the king, actually performed the sacrifice. The sin was Saul’s refusal to wait the full appointed time—his impatience and his acting on his own responsibility irrespective of God’s positive command through Samuel. Saul had waited “seven days” but did not wait till the *end* of the seventh day. Josephus says “he did not fully obey the command.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/13.htm)

**Gill:** Saul waited until the seventh day but not to its close. He was impatient, saw the people deserting, and was unwilling to engage in battle without first sacrificing. Gill notes that in this unsettled time (tabernacle, altar, and ark at different places), some thought non-priests might offer at high places where the tabernacle was not. Saul’s sin was not waiting the full time. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/13.htm)

**Precept Austin / James Smith:** Saul’s duty was plain from 1 Sam 10:8—“Seven days shall thou tarry, till I come to thee, and show thee what thou shalt do.” His faith was tested as day by day he saw Israel’s strength melting away. Every hour seemed to make his case more hopeless. His failure was great because he had waited till *almost* the close of the seventh day—but through pressure of circumstances, his patience with God’s will broke down. He chose his own way and stepped out of God’s favour. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-13-commentary)

---

## vv. 10–12 — Samuel Arrives; Saul’s Excuses

**Traditional reading:** Just as Saul finished offering the burnt offering, Samuel arrived. Saul went out to greet him (the Hebrew implies Saul intended to “bless” Samuel—acting as if he were a priest). Samuel asked, “What have you done?” Saul responded with a cascade of excuses: (1) the troops were deserting, (2) Samuel didn’t come at the appointed time, (3) the Philistines were gathering at Michmash, (4) he feared attack before seeking the LORD’s favour, and (5) he “felt compelled” to offer the sacrifice.

**Guzik:** If Saul had trusted God and waited *one more hour*, everything would have been different. The last moments of waiting are the most difficult and tempt us most powerfully to take matters into our own hands. Saul’s response is a classic example of excuse-making: he blamed the troops, blamed Samuel, blamed the Philistines—all while missing the bottom line that he disobeyed God. Saying “I felt compelled” shows he was ruled by feelings rather than obedience. His entire manner shows this was no misunderstanding—he knew exactly what he had done. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-13/)

**Gill:** Samuel knew by prophetic spirit what Saul had done. Saul tried to lay blame on Samuel: “you did not come within the days appointed.” But the fault was Saul’s impatience—the seventh day had come but not gone. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/13.htm)

**Precept Austin / James Smith:** Saul’s excuse was vain. “Because I saw…I forced myself.” His army dwindling, the Philistine host increasing, Samuel long in coming, his patience exhausted—yet no argument can extenuate the guilt of doing what we know is contrary to God’s mind. The most melancholy feature: there are no signs of repentance. After Samuel’s solemn warning, Saul simply proceeds to number the people (v. 15). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-13-commentary)

**Desiring God (Piper):** At the root of Saul’s insecurity was pride—an excessive desire for others to see him as impressive. This insecurity led to great disobedience. Saul feared the people more than he feared God. “We obey the one we fear.” Saul was remorseful later but never repentant. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/you-obey-the-one-you-fear)

---

## vv. 13–14 — Samuel’s Judgment: The Kingdom Torn Away

**Traditional reading:** Samuel declared, “You have acted foolishly.” This is not about intelligence but moral and spiritual folly—the “fool” in OT wisdom literature is one who lives as if there is no God. Saul had not kept the LORD’s command. If he had obeyed, God would have established his dynasty forever. But now his kingdom would not endure; the LORD had sought “a man after His own heart” (David) and appointed him as ruler.

**Guzik:** “Foolishly” (Hebrew *sakal*) is stronger than it sounds in English—it denotes moral and spiritual deficiency, not mere silliness. The bottom line was disobedience. God told Saul his dynasty was finished. Yet Saul reigned another ~20 years; the judgment was not immediate removal but the *certainty* of the dynasty’s end. This was also an invitation to repentance—God’s threatenings, like His promises, are often conditional. Poole: “Though God threaten Saul with the loss of his kingdom for this sin, yet it is not improbable that there was a tacit condition implied.” Guzik then contrasts Saul (a man after Israel’s heart—image, prestige, what men look at) with David (a man after God’s heart—honouring God, enthroning God as king, having a soft repentant heart, loving people). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-13/)

**Gill:** Saul is not charged with intruding into the priest’s office but with not waiting the full time—showing impatience, disregard for Samuel, and distrust of God. “It matters not whether the thing commanded is greater or less, it is disobedience to the command that is the sin.” This might seem a small thing, but being against God’s command, it was sinful and severely chastised—especially as Saul was the first king and made an example for all succeeding kings. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/13.htm)

**Ellicott:** Saul’s deeper sin was his determination to act independently of God’s revealed will. He thought Israel could do without supernatural assistance. He reserved the right to act in emergencies without—or even contrary to—divine direction. The twice-repeated assertion “Thou hast not kept the commandment of the LORD” (vv. 13–14), uncontradicted by Saul, shows this was overt rebellion. Yet even then Saul might have repented; God’s threatenings are conditional. “Had King Saul repented what he had done, he might have been forgiven…But behind it stands the Divine foreknowledge and omnipotence, and so to the prophetic view Saul’s refusal to repent…and the succession of David were all revealed as accomplished facts.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/13.htm)

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** Samuel charged Saul with foolishness for disobedience. The Lord had raised up Saul to please the people as their king, *but not to represent them in the mediatorship of a priest*. If Saul had been obedient, his kingdom would have been established. The reference to “a man after His own heart”—so often applied to David—appears here for the first time. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-samuel-13.html)

**Precept Austin / James Smith:** Saul’s loss was deplorable. He turned away from the Lord; now the Lord seeks another. “All Saul’s trumpeting and planning now can no more hinder the kingdom from settling down in David than he could hinder the sun from setting in the west. He may shake himself like Samson, but the power is gone.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-13-commentary)

**“A man after His own heart” — key interpretations:**

- **Guzik:** Someone who (1) honours the LORD above his own will, (2) enthrones God as king rather than self, (3) has a soft, repentant heart (David confessed; Saul excused), and (4) loves other people. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-13/)
- **Gill:** A man “every way agreeable to the will of God, and who would fulfil his will”—David, though Samuel did not yet know who he was. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/13.htm)
- **Ellicott:** David was probably a mere child when these words were spoken. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/13.htm)

---

## vv. 15–16 — Samuel Departs; Saul Numbers His Men

**Traditional reading:** Samuel left Gilgal and went up to Gibeah in Benjamin. Saul numbered the remaining troops—only about 600 men (down from 3,000 in v. 2). Saul, Jonathan, and the troops stayed in Geba of Benjamin, while the Philistines camped at Michmash.

**Guzik:** Samuel left probably knowing the announcement of judgment was an invitation to repentance, and probably also knowing Saul would not repent. Saul’s force shrank from 3,000 to 600—God allowed this to test whether Saul believed God could deliver from so many with so few. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-13/)

**Gill:** Samuel arose “seemingly in wrath and displeasure,” not staying to offer the remaining peace offerings. Saul either went with him or quickly followed. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/13.htm)

---

## vv. 17–18 — Philistine Raiding Parties

**Traditional reading:** Raiders went out from the Philistine camp in three divisions: one toward Ophrah in the land of Shual, one toward Beth-horon, and one toward the border road overlooking the Valley of Zeboim facing the wilderness.

**Guzik:** With so many troops, the Philistines could raid at will—a fearless and fearsome army against Saul and Israel. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-13/)

**Ellicott:** These raiding parties show the Philistines’ confidence and their strategy of devastating the countryside to weaken Israel before a decisive battle. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_samuel/13/)

---

## vv. 19–22 — The Philistine Iron Monopoly

**Traditional reading:** There was no blacksmith in all Israel because the Philistines wanted to prevent the Hebrews from making swords or spears. Israelites had to go down to the Philistines even to sharpen their agricultural tools—plowshares, mattocks, axes, and sickles. The Philistines charged a *pim* (about two-thirds of a shekel) for sharpening various tools. Consequently, on the day of battle, no sword or spear was found among the troops—only Saul and Jonathan had weapons.

**Guzik:** The Philistines had superior military technology as a seafaring people who traded with technologically advanced cultures (especially Greeks). They imported iron weapons and guarded the technology carefully. Archaeologists have unearthed numerous iron artifacts from this period, leading to the consensus that iron was introduced into Canaan by the Philistines (Youngblood). The technological gap underscores that Israel could only win by trusting God completely—making Saul’s faithlessness all the more destructive. A *pim* was about two-thirds of a shekel. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-13/)

**Gill:** The Philistines deliberately prevented Israel from having blacksmiths so they could not manufacture weapons. This kept Israel defenceless and subservient. (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/13.htm)

**Precept Austin:** Wikipedia (cited) notes that Josephus attributes this to a systematic seizure of iron items by the Philistines in the region of Gibeah. None of the soldiers carried swords or spears and had to rely on axes, sickles, mattocks, and plow points as weapons. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-13-commentary)

---

## v. 23 — The Philistine Garrison at the Pass

**Traditional reading:** A garrison of the Philistines went out to the pass at Michmash—setting the stage for Jonathan’s bold action in the next chapter.

**Guzik:** This verse transitions to ch. 14 where Jonathan and his armour-bearer will launch a daring attack on this very pass. The Philistines controlled the strategic high ground. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-13/)

---

## Traditions Compared

Given the search and fetch limits, I was only able to retrieve material from these perspectives:

| Tradition | Source(s) Found | Key Distinctive in This Chapter |
|-----------|----------------|-------------------------------|
| **Pentecostal / Charismatic** | Enduring Word (David Guzik) | Emphasises the test of faith in the “last moments of waiting,” spiritual warfare parallels, and the Holy Spirit’s role in conviction vs. excuse-making |
| **Reformed Baptist** | Desiring God (John Piper) | Stresses that Saul feared people more than God; insecurity as pride; obedience as evidence of whom we truly fear |
| **Baptist (General)** | Gill, Garner-Howes | Focus on the precise nature of the disobedience (not priestly usurpation but impatience); the conditional nature of God’s threatenings |
| **Anglican (older)** | Ellicott | Detailed historical and textual analysis; argues Saul’s sin was not offering the sacrifice himself but refusing to wait for God’s timing and acting independently of divine direction |
| **Evangelical (broad)** | Precept Austin (Wiersbe, James Smith, Brian Bell, NET notes) | “Slippery slope” framework; the testing of faith; detailed textual notes on v. 1 |

**What I was unable to retrieve (due to search/fetch limits):**
- Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org)
- Methodist/Wesleyan (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com)
- Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com)
- Orthodox (oca.org)
- Modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org full notes)
- Spurgeon sermons specifically on this chapter (spurgeon.org)

For Catholic and Orthodox readings, one would typically find emphasis on Saul’s sin as a violation of the proper distinction between kingly and priestly office—a theme important in Catholic sacramental theology. For Lutheran readings, the law/gospel distinction would frame Saul’s failure to trust God’s promise versus his attempt to secure favour by works. For modern scholarship, the NET Bible notes and Bible Odyssey would discuss the textual problems in v. 1, the archaeology of the Philistine iron monopoly, and the Deuteronomistic historian’s theological shaping of the narrative.
